second-agricultural-revolution-s1.title: Farming and food in Country A, 1750 to 1900

table.caption: Farm work, food and towns in Country A, 1750 to 1900 (invented data for practice)
cols: Share of people living in towns

second-agricultural-revolution-s2.title: A new machine for the harvest, 1831
second-agricultural-revolution-s2.text: LevlPrep summary, 2026, based on US farm histories. In 1831, Cyrus McCormick showed a horse-drawn reaper in Virginia. Before it, workers cut wheat by hand with a scythe or cradle, and a crew could harvest only a few acres a day. Pulled by horses, the reaper cut grain as it moved, so a few people could harvest many times more land in a day. By the 1850s, reapers were being sold across the wheat lands of the US Midwest.

items.q: Which statement describes the trend in the table from 1750 to 1900?
options: Each farm worker grew more food while the share of farm workers fell
Each farm worker grew less food as more people took up farming
The share of people in towns fell while farm output per worker rose
The share of workers in farming stayed about the same over 150 years

why.correct: Read each column from top to bottom: farming's share of workers falls, food per farm worker rises and the share of people in towns rises.
options: Right: food per farm worker rose from 100 to 320 while the share in farming fell from 75% to 25%.
Both parts are reversed: food per worker rose and the share in farming fell.
The share in towns rose, from 15% to 60%.
It fell by 50 percentage points, from 75% to 25%.

items.q: By what percent did food grown per farm worker increase from 1750 to 1900?

mistakes.why: That is the 1900 index value. The increase is the change (320 - 100 = 220) divided by the starting value (100), times 100.

items.q: Which explanation best links the farming columns to the rise in the share of people living in towns?
options: Farms needed more workers, so towns shrank as people moved out
Town growth caused each farm worker to grow less food
Fewer workers were needed on farms, so many moved to town jobs
Food ran short, so people left farms to find food in towns

why.correct: This is the Second Agricultural Revolution's key effect: more food from fewer farmers freed labor for town and factory work.
options: The table shows towns growing, not shrinking.
Food per farm worker rose, not fell.
Right: as each worker grew more food, farms needed fewer hands, and people moved to towns to work, often in factories.
Food per farm worker rose sharply; the table shows no shortage.

items.q: What is one limit of using this table to study farming in Country A?
options: It gives no data on the share of workers in farming
It shows data from a single year
It shows just the share of people who live in towns and cities
National figures hide differences between regions of the country

why.correct: A national table summarizes the whole country. Some regions may have mechanized early and others late; data at a smaller scale would be needed to see that.
options: It does: the second column.
It shows four years, from 1750 to 1900.
It shows three different measures.
Right: the table is at the national scale, so it cannot show which regions changed fastest.

items.q: The reaper in the passage is an example of what?
options: Domestication
Mechanization
Shifting cultivation
The Columbian Exchange

why.correct: Mechanization means replacing human and animal labor with machines, a core part of the Second Agricultural Revolution.
options: Domestication changes wild plants and animals into crops and livestock; the reaper is a machine.
Right: a machine took over work that people had done by hand.
Shifting cultivation is clearing forest plots in turn, not using machines.
The Columbian Exchange moved crops and animals between hemispheres.

items.q: According to the passage, how did the reaper change the work of the harvest?
options: Wheat could be grown in places with no rain
Farmers no longer needed horses to farm
A small crew could harvest many more acres in a day
Each acre of wheat produced twice as much grain

why.correct: The reaper raised output per worker at harvest time. It saved labor rather than growing more grain on each acre.
options: The passage is about harvesting, not water.
The reaper was pulled by horses.
Right: the passage says a few people could harvest many times more land in a day.
The reaper made cutting faster; it did not change how much grain grew on an acre.

items.q: As machines like the reaper spread across the Midwest, what was the most likely effect on farm families' children?
options: Many left for town jobs because farms needed fewer workers
More of them stayed on farms because harvests needed more hands
They moved to the rainforest to practice shifting cultivation
They stopped growing wheat and started herding instead

why.correct: Fewer farm jobs pushed people off the land, while factory jobs pulled them to towns: farming change and migration are linked.
options: Right: labor-saving machines meant fewer jobs on farms, a push toward towns and factories.
Machines reduced the number of hands needed.
Nothing in the change pushed families to the tropics.
Reapers made wheat cheaper to harvest, so wheat spread.

items.q: When and where did the Second Agricultural Revolution begin?
options: In the Fertile Crescent, about 10,000 years ago
In Britain and western Europe, in the 1700s
In South Asia and Mexico, in the 1960s
In the Andes, soon after 1492

why.correct: The Second Agricultural Revolution began in Britain and western Europe in the 1700s, alongside the rise of factories, and spread to North America in the 1800s.
options: That is the First Agricultural Revolution.
Right: new rotations, breeding and tools spread there from the 1700s, then to North America in the 1800s.
Later changes to grain farming in South Asia and Mexico came in the 1960s; the Second Agricultural Revolution was much earlier.
The Andes was a hearth of the potato, not of this revolution.

items.q: In the four-field rotation used in Norfolk, England, in the 1700s, why was clover planted in one field each year?
options: It could be sold abroad for the highest price
It was the one crop that grew well in England's climate
It shaded the soil so weeds could not grow
It fed animals and put nitrogen back into the soil

why.correct: Rotating wheat, turnips, barley and clover kept every field busy and fed animals through winter. Clover added nitrogen, a nutrient wheat needs.
options: Clover was mostly grazed by farm animals, not sold abroad.
Wheat, barley and turnips grew there too.
Its main jobs were feed and restoring nitrogen to the soil.
Right: clover fed livestock and restored the soil, so no field had to lie empty.

items.q: Turnips and clover in the new rotations fed more animals through the winter. What was a likely effect on people's diets in England?
options: More meat, milk and other animal foods
Fewer animals, because land went to crops
A diet of grain alone, with no animal foods
Less food overall, because rotation wore out the soil

why.correct: Better feed meant larger herds and better diets, one reason people in Britain grew healthier and lived longer.
options: Right: more animals kept through winter meant more meat and dairy.
Feed crops let farmers keep more animals, not fewer.
Animal foods increased.
Rotation protected the soil and raised output.

items.q: How did the Second Agricultural Revolution help move Britain from stage 2 toward stage 3 of the demographic transition model in the 1800s?
options: It raised death rates by spreading new diseases from the Americas
It raised birth rates by creating more farm jobs for children
Better diets lowered death rates, and fewer farm jobs led families to towns
It ended migration, so the population stayed in rural areas

why.correct: Linking units: more and better food lowers death rates; as farms need fewer hands and families move to towns, birth rates later fall. Real countries only roughly fit the model.
options: More food lowered death rates; the diseases of the Columbian Exchange hit the Americas hardest.
It cut farm jobs, which over time lowered the value of large families.
Right: more food cut deaths (stage 2); later, town life and less need for child labor on farms helped birth rates fall (stage 3).
It pushed many people from rural areas to towns.

items.q: In the 1700s and 1800s, landowners in England fenced shared village fields and commons into private farms. What was a major effect of this enclosure?
options: Village fields were split into narrow strips running from rivers
Farmers returned to hunting and gathering on the commons
Each family received a square section of 640 acres
Larger farms adopted new methods, but many small farmers lost land

why.correct: Enclosure had positive and negative effects: more productive farms, and also landless families who moved to towns for work.
options: Strips from rivers are long lots, a French survey method in North America.
Enclosure ended shared use of the commons; it did not bring back foraging.
Square sections are part of the US township and range survey.
Right: enclosure allowed new rotations and breeding on larger farms, and it pushed many rural families off the land.

items.q: Which were part of the Second Agricultural Revolution? Select all that apply.
options: Crop rotation with turnips and clover
Machines such as the seed drill and the reaper
The first domestication of wheat and barley
Clearing and burning rainforest plots in turn
Moving the potato from the Andes to Europe by ship

why.correct: The Second Agricultural Revolution brought new rotations, selective breeding, enclosure and machines, first in Britain and then in North America.
options: Right: the Norfolk four-field rotation spread in the 1700s.
Right: mechanization was central to it.
That happened thousands of years earlier, in the First Agricultural Revolution.
That is shifting cultivation, an old extensive system.
That was the Columbian Exchange, after 1492.

items.q: Put these changes in farming in order, from earliest to most recent.
options: First domestication of wheat in the Fertile Crescent
The potato reaches Europe from the Andes
Norfolk four-field rotation spreads in England
Horse-drawn reapers sell across the US Midwest

why.correct: About 10,000 years ago; the late 1500s; the 1700s; the 1850s.

items.q: Build an explanation of how mechanization changed a named region.

why.correct: Place, cause and effect joined by "so": the link between mechanization and migration to towns.

specific.frame: In ___ in the 1800s, ___ meant farms needed fewer workers, so ___.
specific.model: In the US Midwest in the 1800s, machines such as the reaper meant farms needed fewer workers, so many young people moved to towns and cities for factory jobs.

place.label: Place
options: the US Midwest
the Amazon basin

why.1: The Amazon basin was not mechanized in the 1800s.

cause.label: Cause
options: machines such as the reaper
shifting cultivation

why.1: Shifting cultivation is hand farming in forests, not mechanization.

effect.label: Effect
options: many young people moved to towns and cities for factory jobs
more children were needed to work on farms

why.1: Machines replaced farm workers; fewer were needed.
